\title{Estimator Choice Dominates Sampling Error in\\ Correlation-over-Features Interpretability Studies}
\author{Pavan Kumar Dubasi}
\date{4 September 2026}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
A common move in sparse-autoencoder interpretability is to compute one score per feature, one
outcome per feature, and report a partial correlation over a few thousand features. The estimator
for that correlation involves choices that are rarely stated: what to control for, whether to
residualise on ranks or on raw values, and which rank statistic to use. We take one such study end
to end and enumerate them. The study asks whether SAE features that are redundant within a model
are the ones that recur across models, a prediction from natural-latent theory that we expected to
hold, and our first analysis reported a moderate positive. Across 45 defensible specifications the
same correlation ranges from $-0.178$ to $+0.025$, a spread ten times the sampling standard error
of any one estimate. We are unable to find a specification-independent sign. Two of the
specifications were bugs and we fixed them. After the fixes, a position-shuffle null that our own
plan had pre-registered and our analysis had not run absorbed what was left: what predicts
co-firing transfer is how broadly a feature fires, not its redundancy structure. We cannot say how
far this extends beyond ridge-$R^2$ predictors and residualised partial correlations. The
per-feature arrays and the CPU scripts are released.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Interpretability papers increasingly test hypotheses of the form ``feature-level property $X$
predicts feature-level property $Y$'' by computing both over a few thousand sparse-autoencoder
features and reporting a partial correlation \citep{lan2024quantifying, paulo2025different,
gurnee2024universal}. The pipeline is cheap, the sample size is large, and the resulting
confidence intervals are narrow. This paper is about what those narrow intervals do not cover.

Between the arrays and the reported number sit several choices. Which nuisance variables enter the
control set. Whether the variables are rank-transformed before residualisation or after. Which
rank statistic is applied to the residuals. None of these is a bug, and a methods section that
states only the one chosen is not dishonest. But each choice moves the estimate, and if the
movement is large relative to the error bar, then the error bar is answering a question nobody
asked.

We measured that movement on a study of our own. The study asks whether SAE features that are
redundant within a single model are the ones that transfer to an independently trained model. The
question comes from natural-latent theory \citep{wentworth2025natural}, which predicts that latents
recoverable from disjoint parts of a system are the ones that are stable across observers. We
believed the prediction, and our first analysis produced a moderate positive correlation
consistent with it.

Enumerating the estimator choices instead of defending one gives Figure~\ref{fig:spec}. On the
near model pair, the correlation between redundancy and cross-model decoder geometry runs from
$-0.178$ to $+0.025$ across 45 specifications that a referee would accept, and eight of the 45 are
positive. The standard error of any single one of those estimates is $0.020$. The spread is ten
standard errors wide. Across all six cells of the study the spread runs from four to thirteen
standard errors. The study was never short of data. It was short of a decision rule.

Two of the 45 specifications turned out to be defects rather than choices, and we document both.
One is an unfloored ridge $R^2$ that diverges for low-variance features. The other is
residualising on raw skewed controls instead of on ranks. Both are the kind of thing that is
invisible in a methods section and decisive in a result. Separately, our own measurement plan
pre-registered a position-shuffle null that the headline was required to beat, and our
confirmatory analysis did not run it. When we ran it, it absorbed the surviving positive.

Negative and reliability results of this shape are scarce in interpretability. We know of a few:
\citet{kantamneni2025sae} find that SAE probes fail to beat simple baselines,
\citet{heap2025sparse} find that automated interpretability metrics do not distinguish trained from
random transformers, and \citet{paulo2025different} find that SAEs trained on identical data learn
different features. Outside machine learning the corresponding methodology is mature:
\citet{simmons2011false} named the researcher degrees of freedom, \citet{steegen2016multiverse}
proposed reporting every defensible analysis rather than one, and \citet{simonsohn2020specification}
formalised that as the specification curve. We are applying an old tool to a new pipeline. The
finding is that the pipeline needs it.

Contributions:

\begin{itemize}
\item A specification curve over a real correlation-over-features interpretability analysis,
      showing an estimator spread of four to thirteen sampling standard errors and one sign flip
      (Section~\ref{sec:curve}).
\item Two named, reproducible estimator defects, with a regression test for one and a sensitivity
      curve quantifying the other (Section~\ref{sec:defects}).
\item A worked case of a pre-registered null that was not enforced and that absorbs the headline
      when it is (Section~\ref{sec:null}).
\item An audit of our own released arrays that surfaces five further problems, including a control
      variable that is constant on one model pair (Section~\ref{sec:audit}).
\item The per-feature arrays and CPU scripts, so a reader can move any of these numbers themselves.
\end{itemize}

\section{The study}
\label{sec:study}

We state the setup only far enough to make the estimator choices legible. The full configuration
is in Appendix~\ref{app:setup}.

\paragraph{The prediction.} Natural-latent theory \citep{wentworth2025natural} defines a latent
$\Lambda$ over parts $X_1, X_2$ of a system by two conditions: mediation, $X_1 \perp X_2 \mid
\Lambda$, and redundancy, $\Lambda$ is recoverable from each part alone. Latents satisfying both
are argued to be approximately isomorphic across observers who agree on the observable
distribution, hence translatable. Neither condition is new in itself: mediation is conditional
independence with $\Lambda$ in the screening-off role of a common cause \citep{pearl2009causality},
and redundancy is approximate recoverability in the sense of \citet{cover2006elements}, distinct
from the redundant-information term of partial information decomposition
\citep{williams2010nonnegative}. Read as a prediction about SAE features, it says that the most
redundant features in one model should be the ones with counterparts in another. That is the
prediction we set out to test. It is the vehicle for this paper, not its subject.

\paragraph{The predictor.} For each SAE feature $f$ in model A, split A's residual stream into two
halves by dimension parity and set $\mathrm{redundancy}(f) = \min(R^2_{L \to f}, R^2_{R \to f})$,
where $R^2_{H \to f}$ is an in-sample ridge $R^2$ predicting $f$'s activation from a
unit-variance PCA summary of the opposite half, floored at $-1$. The predictor uses model A alone
and no other SAE feature, so it cannot be circular with a co-firing outcome.

\paragraph{The outcomes.} Features are matched across models by token-level max-activation
correlation, a third channel independent of either outcome. The matching is then read two ways.
$U_{\text{dec}}$ is the cross-model decoder cosine after a least-squares alignment of B's decoder
space onto A's. $U_{\text{overlap}}$ is the Jaccard overlap of the two features' top-50 activating
context sets.

\paragraph{The pairs.} GPT-2-small with Pythia-70m-deduped (near), Gemma-2-9b-it with
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (far), and Mistral-7B with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (far). One layer and one
public SAE per model, 2500 features scored per pair.

\paragraph{The statistic.} A partial rank correlation of predictor against outcome, controlling for
firing frequency, activation magnitude and decoder norm. Six cells: three pairs by two outcomes.

That last paragraph is where this paper lives. ``A partial rank correlation, controlling for three
nuisance variables'' does not specify a number.

\section{The specification curve}
\label{sec:curve}

\subsection{The choices}

Three axes, each a decision the original analysis actually faced.

\emph{Residualisation.} Rank-transform the predictor, the outcome and the controls, then
residualise the ranked predictor and outcome on the ranked controls by ordinary least squares. Or
residualise the raw values on the raw controls and rank afterwards. Or use no controls.

\emph{Final statistic.} Pearson, Spearman or Kendall $\tau_b$ on the residuals.

\emph{Control subset.} Any of the eight subsets of \{frequency, magnitude, decoder norm\}.

With the residualisation axis collapsing when the control set is empty, this is $7 \times 2 \times
3 + 3 = 45$ specifications per cell and 270 in total. The pre-registered estimator is
(ranks, Pearson, all three controls). The estimator our original harness used is
(raw, Spearman, all three controls).

\subsection{The result}

Table~\ref{tab:curve} gives the range per cell. Figure~\ref{fig:spec} plots it.

\begin{table}[t]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{llrrrrrr}
\toprule
Pair & Outcome & Pre-reg. & Harness & Min & Max & Range & Range / SE \\
\midrule
near     & decoder   & $-0.122$ & $+0.001$ & $-0.178$ & $+0.025$ & $0.203$ & $10.1$ \\
near     & co-firing & $+0.291$ & $+0.413$ & $+0.215$ & $+0.475$ & $0.261$ & $13.0$ \\
Gemma    & decoder   & $-0.169$ & $-0.162$ & $-0.192$ & $-0.087$ & $0.105$ & $5.3$ \\
Gemma    & co-firing & $+0.005$ & $+0.017$ & $+0.005$ & $+0.129$ & $0.124$ & $6.2$ \\
Mistral  & decoder   & $-0.159$ & $-0.177$ & $-0.182$ & $-0.105$ & $0.078$ & $3.9$ \\
Mistral  & co-firing & $+0.169$ & $+0.308$ & $+0.126$ & $+0.362$ & $0.236$ & $11.8$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Partial correlation of the redundancy score with each universality outcome, across 45
estimator specifications per cell, $N=2500$ features per pair. SE is the analytic standard error
of a partial rank correlation at $N=2500$ with three controls, $0.0200$. The near-pair decoder
cell is the only one that changes sign; eight of its 45 specifications are positive.}
\label{tab:curve}
\end{table}

Three things stand out.

\paragraph{The spread is not sampling noise.} The narrowest cell spreads over four standard errors
and the widest over thirteen. A feature bootstrap on any single specification gives a 95\%
interval about $0.08$ wide. The near-pair decoder cell spreads over $0.20$. Collecting more
features would shrink the interval and leave the spread untouched.

\paragraph{One cell changes sign.} On the near pair the decoder correlation is negative under 37
specifications and positive under eight. We are unable to state a specification-independent sign
for that cell. The two far pairs are negative under all 45, which is a stronger statement than we
could have made from the pre-registered estimator alone, and it is a statement we only get by
running the curve.

\paragraph{The control set alone is enough.} Holding residualisation and statistic at the
pre-registered setting and varying only which controls enter:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lr}
\toprule
Control subset & near-pair decoder $\rho$ \\
\midrule
none                                   & $-0.022$ \\
frequency                              & $-0.020$ \\
magnitude                              & $-0.118$ \\
decoder norm                           & $-0.034$ \\
frequency + magnitude                  & $-0.171$ \\
frequency + decoder norm               & $-0.000$ \\
magnitude + decoder norm               & $-0.068$ \\
frequency + magnitude + decoder norm   & $-0.122$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The same arrays, the same statistic, and the same three candidate confounds give anything from
$-0.000$ to $-0.171$ depending on which two of the three a paper decides to name. Decoder norm is
the most surprising entry. As Section~\ref{sec:audit} shows, it is close to constant, and it still
moves the estimate by 2.4 standard errors.

\subsection{Power was never the problem}

At $N=2500$ with three controls, the standard error is $0.0200$, and the minimum detectable effect
at 80\% power is $0.068$ at $\alpha=0.01$ and $0.083$ at $\alpha=0.001$. The decoder cells, at
$-0.12$ to $-0.17$, clear both. Five of six cells reach the floor of a 1000-shuffle permutation
test, that is $p < 0.001$, and survive Holm-Bonferroni correction across the six cells at
$\alpha=0.01$; the Gemma co-firing cell does not ($p = 0.836$). The original manuscript reported
$p = 0.001$, which is the floor of the procedure and not an estimate; $p < 0.001$ is the correct
form.

We note this because a reader might reasonably suspect the instability is small-sample noise. It
is not. Every specification in the curve is individually well powered, and they disagree anyway.

\section{Two of the specifications were defects}
\label{sec:defects}

Two entries in the curve are not choices in retrospect. They are things we got wrong. Both are
worth naming because both are invisible from a methods section.

\paragraph{An unfloored ridge $R^2$.} For a feature whose activation has a large mean and small
residual variance, $R^2 = 1 - \mathrm{ss\_res} / \mathrm{ss\_tot}$ has a tiny denominator, so any
imperfect fit returns a large negative number. On Gemma-scale and Llama-scale activations the mean
redundancy $R^2$ in our harness reached about $-1.4 \times 10^5$. Those degenerate scores then
correlate with whatever they are asked to correlate with, and the near-pair decoder cell reported
$+0.27$. Flooring $R^2$ at $-1$ removes it. A regression test
(\texttt{test\_harness\_bug.py}) constructs the large-mean, low-variance case, fails on the pre-fix
path at $-3.5 \times 10^4$ and passes on the floored path.

The released arrays are post-floor, so a reader cannot regenerate the $+0.27$. Rather than ask for
trust, we measured how fragile the cell is to that class of corruption. Sending a fraction of
features to the bottom of the predictor ranking, which is what an unfloored blow-up does under a
rank statistic, and choosing the features by highest activation magnitude, which is the class the
blow-up hit:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrr}
\toprule
Fraction of the 2500 features corrupted & 0 & 0.5\% & 1\% & 2\% & 5\% \\
\midrule
near-pair decoder $\rho$ & $-0.122$ & $-0.089$ & $-0.069$ & $-0.051$ & $-0.033$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Twelve features out of 2500 cut the coefficient by a quarter. This is a simulation of the
mechanism on the released arrays, not a reconstruction of the historical number, and it does not
reach $+0.27$ because the historical defect also affected the alignment step.

\paragraph{Residualising on raw skewed controls.} With the floor in place, residualising raw
predictor and raw outcome on the raw controls and then taking Spearman of the residuals gives
$+0.001$ on the near-pair decoder cell. The rank-based partial on the identical arrays gives
$-0.122$. The corrected near-zero that replaced the $+0.27$ was itself an artifact of the
partialling convention. This one is fully regenerable from the release.

\paragraph{The whole pilot table is one estimator away.} Our pre-registration recorded six
non-confirmatory pilot values, including a near-pair co-firing correlation of $+0.41$ that we later
retracted. All six are reproduced to two decimals by applying the raw-residualisation estimator to
the released arrays: $+0.001$, $+0.413$, $-0.162$, $+0.017$, $-0.177$, $+0.308$, against
pre-registered values of $-0.122$, $+0.291$, $-0.169$, $+0.005$, $-0.159$, $+0.169$. The retracted
number is not a mystery. It is what these arrays give under one documented convention, and a reader
can regenerate it.

\section{The null we did not run}
\label{sec:null}

Our measurement plan pre-registered a second control, stronger than the feature-pairing permutation
test, and our confirmatory analysis did not enforce it. For each context, permute token positions
independently before splitting the residual stream into halves, then recompute the redundancy
score. This preserves which contexts a feature fires in and how strongly, and destroys the
within-context positional structure. The shuffled score therefore isolates the context-breadth
component of redundancy. The registered standard was that the headline had to beat this null.

It does not (Table~\ref{tab:null}, Figure~\ref{fig:null}). On every pair the shuffled predictor
associates with co-firing at least as strongly as the real one, the two scores are rank-correlated
at $0.64$ to $0.86$, and the incremental partial of redundancy given the shuffled score is
indistinguishable from zero or negative on all three co-firing cells. The reverse incremental
retains signal. Feature-bootstrap intervals on $|\text{real}| - |\text{null}|$ are negative on all
three co-firing cells: near $[-0.124, -0.058]$, Gemma $[-0.099, -0.011]$, Mistral
$[-0.072, -0.018]$. The shuffled score is the better predictor.

\begin{table}[t]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{llrrrr}
\toprule
Pair & Outcome & real & shuffle null & real $\mid$ null & null $\mid$ real \\
\midrule
near    & co-firing & $+0.291$ & $+0.382$ & $-0.035$ & $+0.261$ \\
Gemma   & co-firing & $+0.005$ & $+0.081$ & $-0.086$ & $+0.118$ \\
Mistral & co-firing & $+0.169$ & $+0.213$ & $+0.017$ & $+0.133$ \\
\midrule
near    & decoder   & $-0.122$ & $-0.190$ & $+0.057$ & $-0.157$ \\
Gemma   & decoder   & $-0.169$ & $-0.029$ & $-0.225$ & $+0.153$ \\
Mistral & decoder   & $-0.159$ & $-0.253$ & $+0.044$ & $-0.204$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The pre-registered position-shuffle null, under the pre-registered estimator and control
set. The last two columns are incremental partials of each predictor given the other. The
co-firing association never beats the null and retains nothing beyond it. The null column uses a
single stored shuffle realisation, which is a limitation we discuss in
the Limitations section.}
\label{tab:null}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.72\textwidth]{fig3_null.pdf}
\caption{The position-shuffled predictor tracks co-firing transfer at least as well as the real
one on all three pairs. Destroying within-context positional structure while preserving which
contexts a feature fires in does not weaken the association, so context breadth and not redundancy
structure is what the co-firing correlation is measuring. $N=2500$ features per pair; one stored
shuffle realisation.}
\label{fig:null}
\end{figure}

The interpretation we draw, and it is an interpretation formed after the fact rather than a
pre-registered mechanism claim, is that what predicts co-firing transfer is how broadly a feature
fires across contexts. \citet{paulo2025different} report the same-data analogue: the latents that
fire most often are the ones shared across seed-varied SAEs. \citet{gurnee2024universal} report the
opposite for neurons in seed-varied GPT-2 models, where universal neurons fire sparsely and
selectively. The tension may reflect the unit, the statistic, or the regime, and we do not resolve
it.

The decoder side behaves differently. On the Gemma pair the negative strengthens beyond the null,
with an incremental partial of $-0.225$ and a bootstrap interval of $[-0.262, -0.184]$. On the
other two pairs the unique component is small and of the opposite sign. We do not have an
explanation for that difference, and Section~\ref{sec:audit} gives a reason to be cautious about
the Gemma cell specifically.

There is a lesson here that is separate from the numbers. The paper's own thesis is that a single
undeclared choice can move a headline. Our null was a single stored draw. We caught the first
problem and reproduced the second.

\section{What survives, and under what estimator}
\label{sec:survives}

Under the single pre-registered estimator, with everything above declared:

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.72\textwidth]{fig2_forest.pdf}
\caption{Under the pre-registered estimator, the redundancy score is weakly negatively associated
with cross-model decoder geometry on all three pairs and positively associated with co-firing
overlap on two. Points are partial rank correlations with 95\% feature-bootstrap intervals,
$N=2500$ per pair; the grey band is the widest per-cell permutation null. This is one column of
Figure~\ref{fig:spec}, not a specification-independent result.}
\label{fig:forest}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Decoder geometry.} Weakly negative on all three pairs, $\rho$ between $-0.17$ and
$-0.12$, which is 1.5 to 2.9 percent of variance. Under the pre-registered estimator we do not
find that within-model redundancy predicts cross-model decoder geometry in the direction the
natural-latent reading suggests; we find a small association in the other direction. On the two far
pairs the sign is stable across all 45 specifications. On the near pair it is not.

\paragraph{Co-firing overlap.} Positive on the near pair ($+0.291$) and one far pair ($+0.169$),
inside the permutation null on the other ($+0.005$). Our pre-registered acceptance criterion
required $\rho > +0.20$ on at least two of three pairs. One pair clears it, so the criterion is not
met. More decisively, Section~\ref{sec:null} shows the association does not beat the position
shuffle and retains nothing beyond it.

\paragraph{What we would tell a practitioner.} Do not use a within-model redundancy score as a
cheap screen for which SAE features will transfer, at least not for decoder geometry. Treat breadth
of firing as the first confound to rule out in any transfer-prediction claim. And do not report a
single partial correlation over features without saying what else you could have reported.

\section{An audit of our own release}
\label{sec:audit}

Releasing the per-feature arrays let us audit the arrays rather than the code. Five problems
surfaced, three of which we did not know about when the analysis was written. We report them
because they are the same category of failure as the two named defects, and because a paper about
measurement reliability that hides its own is not worth much.

\paragraph{One control is constant on one pair.} In the Gemma arrays, the firing-frequency column
equals $1.0$ for all 2500 features, to machine precision. The reported analysis states that every
correlation is partialled on frequency, magnitude and decoder norm. On that pair the frequency
column contributes nothing: the three-control partial is $-0.1693$ and the magnitude-only partial
is $-0.1692$. This lands on the one cell we singled out for a redundancy-specific effect.

\paragraph{One control is near-constant on all three.} SAE decoder rows are unit-normalised, so
decoder norm ranges over $2.3 \times 10^{-3}$, $2.9 \times 10^{-7}$ and $8.9 \times 10^{-4}$ on
the three pairs. On the Gemma pair that is floating-point noise. It is still enough to move the
near-pair estimate from $-0.171$ to $-0.122$ when added to the control set, which is the entry in
the control-subset table above.

\paragraph{A pre-registered filter was not applied.} Our frozen measure contract excluded
always-on features, defined as firing in more than 50 percent of contexts. Measured on the released
arrays, 3.0 percent of near-pair features, 6.5 percent of Mistral-pair features and 100 percent of
Gemma-pair features exceed that threshold. Applied as written, the filter would have emptied the
Gemma cell. It was not applied, and the original manuscript did not declare this.

\paragraph{The co-firing outcome has a high floor.} $U_{\text{overlap}}$ takes 38 to 44 distinct
values over 2500 features. Its minimum in all three pairs is exactly six shared contexts out of
50, and no matched pair of features overlaps in fewer. Under independent top-50 draws from 3000
contexts the expected overlap is $0.83$ contexts. The measure therefore sits on a large shared
baseline, consistent with a context-popularity effect and with the position-shuffle result. We
would not now interpret the absolute size of a co-firing correlation.

\paragraph{A load-bearing control is not in the release.} Our defence against ``the decoder
measure is dead, that is why the effect is small'' is that the measure exceeds a shuffled-decoder
baseline in every run. No baseline value and no code that computes one is in the release, so a
reader cannot check it. This is the gap we would close first, and the Limitations section
says what it would cost.

\section{Related work}

\paragraph{Feature universality.} That independently trained networks learn overlapping features is
widely reported \citep{olah2020zoom, towards2024universality} and, at the level of whole
representations rather than individual features, argued for by the Platonic Representation
Hypothesis \citep{huh2024platonic} and measured by tools such as CKA and stitching
\citep{kornblith2019similarity}. On the SAE side \citep{bricken2023monosemanticity},
\citet{lan2024quantifying} measure feature-space universality across models,
\citet{thasarathan2025universal} train a single cross-model SAE that aligns concepts, and
\citet{lindsey2024crosscoders} use crosscoders for model diffing. \citet{paulo2025different} show
that SAEs trained on the same data learn different features, which bounds how much any single-SAE
result can mean. We differ from all of these in asking a reliability question about the estimator
rather than a substantive question about universality.

\paragraph{Controls and illusions.} Our position-shuffle null is in the control-task lineage of
\citet{hewitt2019control}: a statistic earns its interpretation by beating a structure-destroying
control. The interpretability-illusion literature documents what happens when it does not
\citep{bolukbasi2021illusion, makelov2023illusion}, and \citet{heap2025sparse} show that automated
interpretability metrics fail to separate trained from random transformers.
\citet{lan2024quantifying} already use a random-pairing permutation null and filter trivial
high-frequency token features, so permutation nulls in this area are not new; what we add is that
the stronger within-context shuffle absorbs the effect the weaker null let through.

\paragraph{Specification curves.} \citet{simmons2011false} named researcher degrees of freedom.
\citet{steegen2016multiverse} proposed reporting the whole space of defensible analyses rather than
one, and \citet{simonsohn2020specification} formalised the specification curve. We are not aware of
a published specification curve over an SAE feature-level correlation, and the size of the spread
we find suggests there should be more of them.

\paragraph{Negative results in interpretability.} \citet{kantamneni2025sae} are the closest analogue
in shape: a hypothesis about SAEs that did not survive contact with simple baselines, reported as
such. Results of this kind remain scarce, which is part of why we are reporting ours.

\section*{Limitations}


The position-shuffle null is one stored realisation. We cannot quantify variance across shuffle
seeds from the released arrays, because doing so needs the residual-stream activations. This is
the objection we would most want to fix, and it is cheap to fix: one harness rerun per pair with
20 independent permutations, which reuses the cached activations and costs under ten dollars of
cloud GPU in total.

The shuffled-decoder positive control for the decoder measure is not in the release, so the claim
that the decoder measure is alive rests on an unreleased boolean. The same rerun would fix it.

Three pairs, one layer each, one public SAE per model. SAE training is unstable across seeds
\citep{paulo2025different}, so SAE-level variance is entirely unmeasured here and may well be
larger than the estimator variance we do measure. An estimator-variance study that ignores
SAE-seed variance is incomplete, and this one does.

The pairs are confounded. The model on which redundancy is computed is GPT-2-small (base, residual
post, 124M), Gemma-2-9b-it (instruction tuned, residual post, 9B) and Mistral-7B (base, residual
pre, 7B). Tuning, hook point and scale change together across the three pairs, and the partner
model is Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in two of three. No difference between pairs can be attributed to
any one axis. We report within pair and do not compare across pairs.

The redundancy predictor is an in-sample ridge $R^2$ on a PCA summary. It is an operational proxy
for the recoverability condition, not the condition itself, so a null or a negative here bounds the
proxy and not the theorem, whose guarantee requires mediation and redundancy jointly.

The 45 specifications are the ones we could vary on the released arrays. Others exist that we could
not vary: the number of PCA components, the ridge penalty, the top-$K$ of the overlap measure, the
matching channel, the feature filter. The spread we report is therefore a lower bound on the spread
a determined analyst could produce.

The bootstrap resamples individual features rather than the co-firing-clustered groups our plan
specified, so the intervals may be anti-conservative under dependence between co-firing features.

The two defects we document are specific to ridge-$R^2$ predictors and residualised partial
correlations. We cannot say whether other estimator families in interpretability harbour analogous
failure modes; we would guess that they do, and that is a guess.

All findings are correlational. We make no causal claim.

\section*{Reproducibility}


The measure definitions, analysis plan and acceptance thresholds were frozen and committed before
the blocking runs. Every number in this paper regenerates from the released per-feature arrays on
a CPU: \texttt{recompute\_partials.py} for the pre-registered cells and the shuffle null,
\texttt{spec\_curve.py} for the specification curve, \texttt{contamination\_curve.py} for the
corruption sensitivity, \texttt{power\_and\_spread.py} for the standard errors and the
multiple-comparison bookkeeping, \texttt{robustness\_checks.py} for the split-half and Kendall
checks, \texttt{test\_harness\_bug.py} for the ridge floor, and \texttt{make\_figs\_v2.py} for the
figures. The figure scripts recompute their own inputs so that a figure cannot drift from a table.
The arrays hold, per feature: the redundancy score and its position-shuffled counterpart, both
universality outcomes, firing frequency, activation magnitude, decoder norm and the aligned decoder
row. Values that this release cannot regenerate are named in Section~\ref{sec:audit}: the pre-floor
redundancy scores and the shuffled-decoder baseline.

\section*{Ethics}

This work uses publicly released pretrained language models (GPT-2, Pythia, Gemma-2-9b,
Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B), their publicly released sparse autoencoders, and a public corpus
sample. There are no human subjects, no private or personally identifying data, and no new model
weights. One safety-relevant note: predictors of which interpretability findings transfer across
models bear on the argument that auditing a small model informs claims about a larger one. Our
result is that such predictors can be artifacts of the estimator, so transfer claims should come
with a frozen, reproducible measurement pipeline and, we would now add, a specification curve.

\appendix

\section{Experimental setup}
\label{app:setup}

Activations come from 3000 contexts of 64 tokens drawn from a public Pile sample
(\texttt{NeelNanda/pile-10k}), streamed identically for both models of a pair. Models and SAEs are
all publicly released, loaded through \texttt{sae\_lens} and \texttt{transformer\_lens}.

\emph{Near pair:} GPT-2-small, layer 8 residual post (\texttt{gpt2-small-resid-post-v5-32k}) with
Pythia-70m-deduped, layer 4 residual post (\texttt{pythia-70m-deduped-res-sm}).
\emph{Gemma pair:} Gemma-2-9b-it, layer 20 residual post, width 16k canonical
(\texttt{gemma-scope-9b-it-res-canonical}) with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 16 residual post,
Llama-Scope $8\times$ (\texttt{llama\_scope\_lxr\_8x}, \texttt{l16r\_8x}).
\emph{Mistral pair:} Mistral-7B, layer 16 residual pre (\texttt{mistral-7b-res-wg}) with the same
Llama-3.1-8B SAE.

Per pair, the 2500 most active model-A features are scored. Redundancy is
$\min(R^2_{L \to f}, R^2_{R \to f})$, each $R^2$ a closed-form in-sample ridge fit
($\lambda = 1$) predicting the feature's per-context half-mean activation from a 48-dimensional PCA
summary of the opposite residual-stream half, halves taken by dimension parity, floored at $-1$.
Cross-model matching is by token-level max-activation correlation. $U_{\text{overlap}}$ is the
Jaccard overlap of top-50 context sets; the released values lie exactly on the grid $k/(100-k)$
for integer $k$, which confirms this from the arrays alone. $U_{\text{dec}}$ is the aligned
cross-model decoder cosine. The position-shuffle null permutes token positions independently per
context before the half split, and one realisation is stored. Bootstrap and permutation sizes are
1000 throughout.

\section{Specification curve details}
\label{app:curve}

The 45 specifications per cell are the product of the residualisation axis (ranks, raw), the final
statistic (Pearson, Spearman, Kendall $\tau_b$) and the seven non-empty control subsets, plus the
three no-control specifications where the residualisation axis collapses. All 270 values are in
\texttt{results/spec\_curve.json}.

The near-pair decoder cell is the only sign flip. Its extremes are $-0.178$
(ranks, Spearman, frequency + magnitude) and $+0.025$ (raw, Pearson, magnitude + decoder norm).
Six of the eight positive specifications residualise on raw values. The other two residualise on
ranks with a control set that includes decoder norm but not magnitude, and both are within $0.004$
of zero. Rank-residualised specifications on that cell range from $-0.178$ to $+0.004$;
raw-residualised ones range from $-0.035$ to $+0.025$. Dropping magnitude from the control set is
what erases the effect; the residualisation convention is what can invert it.
